item.p: Whom it serves: callers of the regex functions whose regex must spell a literal that the input seldom holds, above all SchXslt: its expansion of abstract patterns calls replace($s, "(\W*)\$name(\W*)", ...) for every parameter on every test expression. Such a regex can match the empty string before a "$", so 's start filter skipped nothing and every position was attempted, though no match exists without "$name": sxml_regex_matcher_scan was 12.9 % of the expand stage.

Mechanism (glossary , ; all in src/regex.c): when a regex is compiled, a CODEPOINT instruction is required when MATCH cannot be reached from the first instruction while avoiding it (the successors the matcher can take: both ways of a split, a counted loop's choice and a character repetition); the CODEPOINT instructions after it then run right after it, so their run is in every match, contiguous. Of the first 16 candidates the longest required run is kept, its first 32 bytes as UTF-8. The instructions reachable without the run read every character a match reads before its first occurrence; their read set is the literal's prefix (a back-reference or "." with s: anything). At search time the scan finds the literal's next occurrence (memchr, memcmp), walks back from it while the characters are in the prefix read set, and skips the positions before that; when the literal does not occur, it skips every position left. A position skipped counts one step within the step limit, as settled (skipped positions of an ASCII string are counted from bytes, otherwise from codepoints). The start filter's first characters became a read set too. Correct because a match starting at p reads the literal at some q' at or after the first occurrence q found from p, and every character in [p, q') is read by a prefix instruction.

What is not required, or not analysed: a regex with lookahead or lookbehind (their regexes read characters a match does not consume) or more than 256 instructions gets none, and the analysis walks a fixed stack (). Alternations, optional parts, repetitions and counted loops follow from the graph (a counted loop's body is never required: its choice may leave). Under flag i a character with case variants is a class, so only characters without variants form a literal; q and x are compiled away first; anchors, \b and multi-line mode read nothing, so they do not change the literal and only restrict the attempts made. sxml_regex_matcher_match_at (XSD pattern facets) is unchanged.
Measured (release, x86_64; valgrind instructions of the process, 10^6, and processor seconds, the fastest runs on a shared machine), before / after:
SchXslt's expand stage of EN 16931 (step bound raised in a scratch build only): 75,266.6 / 65,844.7 (-12.5 %), scan 12.87 % / 0.42 % of it, inclusive; 10.68 / 9.14 s; the same output;
tests/bench/regex-match.xq: 6,152.4 / 6,174.5 (+0.36 %: its literals are found where the start filter already skipped); 0.595 / 0.600 s;
5,000 distinct regexes compiled: 199.6 / 201.8, about 440 instructions more a compile; "(\W*)\$PARAMn(\W*)": 250.5 / 256.8.

Checked: QT4 XP40 and XQ40 fn-analyze-string, fn-matches, fn-matches.re, fn-matching-segments, fn-regex, fn-replace, fn-tokenize and XT40 analyze-string, regex, regex-syntax, regex-syntax-xslt20 with the release drivers: 4,405 pass, 10 fail, 1 wrong error, 1,154 not run, before and after, 0 outcomes differ case by case. 14,400 random regexes (literals, classes, groups, back-references, assertions, anchors, quantifiers; flags i, m, s, q, x) on random inputs of up to 40 characters through fn:analyze-string, and 3,600 in SchXslt's shape through fn:analyze-string, fn:tokenize and fn:replace: the same output, except one search that reached the step limit before and now ends with the right result ([^a].(.+?)+?A\S: the positions after the last "A" are skipped).
Left: a literal inside a counted loop or an assertion is not used; the step limit of a search can now be reached later than before, never sooner.
